subject: babaYagaHut
pitch:
Category: Diorama.
Subject: Baba Yaga's hut on chicken legs.
Style: Slavic folk art.

spec.name: Baba Yaga's Hut on Chicken Legs
spec.description: A Slavic folk-art diorama of Baba Yaga's carved log izba standing on two giant scaly chicken legs in a clearing, ringed by a bone-and-skull fence with glowing eyes.
spec.layout: Diorama on a round earth-and-grass plinth (radius 3.0, top at y=0.15). The hut's log cabin (about 2.3 wide, 2.5 long, 1.4 tall) is lifted on two huge chicken legs to a floor height of y=1.6. It faces +Z. From the front, a plank stair with carved bannisters runs from the door down to the ground between the legs. The door is centred on the front wall under a steep gabled roof. The ridge runs front to back, and the front gable carries a carved pediment with a round window. Konyok (carved horse-head) finials cap both ridge ends. A stone chimney with grey smoke stands at the rear right. Two legs stand left and right (x = ±0.85) with knees forward, hocks back, and three forward toes plus one back toe gripping the ground, each toe ending in a dark claw. Feather pantaloons fluff over each thigh just under the floor beams. A ring of bone fence posts topped with skulls with glowing amber eyes circles the clearing at radius 2.4 and is open in a gap at the front (±35 degrees around +Z) for the path. Mushrooms, stepping stones, a birch tree at back left and a mortar and pestle at front left finish the scene. Folk-art style throughout: bold flat colours (red, blue, yellow, green, cream) painted as small parts on warm wood. Carved platbands around windows and door, saw-tooth and scalloped barge boards, sun and rosette motifs, hearts, and zig-zag borders. Every motif is built from small parts in outline (ink), main colour and highlight layers. Shapes stay chunky and blocky, like a puppet made of primitives.

parts.builds: Both giant chicken legs, mirrored left and right, built skeleton-first on the hipL/kneeL/ankleL/footL chains with sweeps. Each leg has a fat feathered thigh (a pantaloon of overlapping cream feather blades, root featherCream with tips legOrange) tucked under the floor beams at y=1.7. Below the knee the drumstick tapers into a scaly legYellow shin whose forward knee and back-pointing hock are clearly separated. A scale pattern of small legOrange plates and ridge rows runs down the metatarsus, with a spur on the back of the hock. A chunky foot pad leads into three forward toes (fanned apart, the inner one angled toward the centre) and one back toe. They are built as sweeps tapering into dark claw cones (claw) and have knuckle bumps and toe-pad ridges in legOrange. The toes rest flat on the ground top (y=0.15) and sink about 0.02. Leg parts ride hipL..toeBackR. Keep the stair gap between the feet clear: inner toes must not go past x=±0.5.
parts.attaches: Hip tops end at hipL and hipR inside the cabin foundation beams (hutFloor). Feet stand on groundTop at footL and footR.

parts.builds: The izba body, riding the hut joint. Underneath is a foundation frame at y=1.6..1.85 with cross beams and floorboard edge (logDark), sized x ±1.45, z ±1.5, so the leg hips vanish into it. Above are 7 courses of horizontal round logs (cylinders, alternating logLight and a slightly different logDark-tinted course) forming four walls. The wall surfaces sit at x=±1.15 and z=±1.25, spanning y=1.85..3.2. Corner log ends overlap and protrude to about 0.15 past the walls, with end-grain discs (logEnd) with ink ring lines. Moss-and-tow caulking is shown as thin grassDark strips between some courses. The front wall is a full-width solid wall (the door and windows are applied by the facade part on its surface, so do not cut any openings). The back wall has a plain small hatch of logDark boards and a carved carveRed strip. Add the hut's top plate (a flat logDark board ring at y=3.15..3.2) that the roof sits on. Add small carved details: carveYellow notch marks on the corner ends and a few knot-eyes (ink) on the logs.
parts.attaches: Sits on the legs at hutFloor and hipL/hipR. Its top plate meets the roof at eaveLine. The facade is applied to the front wall at z=1.25 and the side wall surfaces at x=±1.15.

parts.builds: Everything applied to the cabin's outside, front and sides. Door: a plank door in logLight and logDark on the door joint, hinge at x=0.42, filling x ±0.42 and y 1.85..2.9. It has an ink outline, iron-style strap hinges (ink), a ring handle, and a carved carveRed and carveYellow sun rosette in its upper half. It sits in a carved platband frame (carveBlue with carveWhite scallops and carveYellow dots), with a pediment hood above bearing a carved heart. A glowing skull lantern (bone skull, glow eyes) hangs above the door. A hand-towel (rushnyk) panel with a carveRed and carveWhite zig-zag pattern hangs beside it. On both side walls, a window with a dark ink pane that glows glow, carveWhite muntins, a carved platband in carveBlue with a carveRed scalloped crown, and two hinged shutters (carveGreen painted with carveYellow flowers). Each side window sits at windowL and windowR. A plank stair rises from the doorBase threshold (a small porch landing at z 1.25..1.55 with carved front edge) down to stairBottom (z 2.5), with 5 treads. Carved bannister posts and rails run on both sides, topped with small konyok-style carved knobs in carveRed and carveYellow. The stair stays within x ±0.5 between the legs. Colours stay bold and flat, with ink outlines under main colours and highlights.
parts.attaches: Front elements are seated on the front wall at z=1.25 (wallFrontCentre, doorBase). The side windows are seated on the side wall surfaces (windowL and windowR, x=±1.15). The stair foot rests on groundTop at stairBottom. The side-window box overflow to x ±1.3 is allowed. Rides the door joint (door) and hut.

parts.builds: A steep two-pitch gabled roof with its ridge along Z, from eave y=3.2 to ridge y=4.45, overhanging to x ±1.65 and z ±1.75. Shingle rows are overlapping flat boards (roofRed and roofWood alternating, with a few carveGreen moss patches on the upper faces), each with rounded or scalloped lower edges. A ridge beam (logDark) runs along the top. Konyok horse-head finials (carved logLight plus carveRed mane notches, ink eye) cap both the front end (ridgeFront) and the back end (ridgeBack). The front gable face is a solid board triangle (logLight vertical planks) at gableFace, with a round attic window (ink ring, glow pane, carveYellow sun rays) and a carved folk fringe (zig-zag barge boards in carveRed, carveBlue and carveWhite) along both front rafter edges, plus a hanging pendant at the apex and rosettes at the eaves. The back gable is plainer boards. A stone chimney (stone with logDark cap and a mortar line pattern) rises at chimneyBase to about y=4.7 with three smoke puffs (smoke, stacked faceted spheres, growing and drifting to +X). It reaches at most y=4.9.
parts.attaches: Sits on the top plate of the cabin at eaveLine (y=3.15..3.2). Everything rides the hut joint.

parts.builds: The diorama base: a low faceted disc of radius 3.0 (y=0..0.15) with a soil side wall (soil) and a grass top (grass) with a slightly irregular rim, rotated facets and a few grassDark patches. A path of 6 flat stone slabs (stone) leads from stairBottom to the front edge between the fence gap. Add scattered grass tufts (blade clusters in grass and grassDark), a few folk-art flowers (carveRed, carveYellow, carveWhite petals on green stems) and some roots/soil mounds at the base of the legs where the claws grip. Add flat stone rim pebbles around the edge. Keep the ground simple, with a flat top at y=0.15 so the toes and fence posts sit on it. Static, no smooth bending.
parts.attaches: Its top is the shared groundTop (y=0.15). The legs' toes, the stair foot and the fence posts all sit on it.

parts.builds: The bone fence and the scene props around the hut. A ring of about 18 posts at radius 2.4 around the clearing, skipping the front gap (within ±35 degrees of +Z, where the path goes). Each post is a long bone (bone cylinder shaft with knobbed ends) set slightly sunk into the ground, alternating heights 0.9..1.3, linked by two horizontal rail bones (bone). Every post is topped by a skull (bone, faceted sphere with jaw box, ink eye sockets with glowing glow pupils, nose notch and teeth row) turned to face inward or toward the viewer, with a few ordinary wood stakes between them. Additional props: a cluster of three fly-agaric mushrooms (mushRed caps with carveWhite dots and carveWhite stems) near the front right fence, a large birch tree (birch trunk with ink bark marks, a few branches, and carveGreen/grassDark leaf clumps) at back left around (-2.0, 0, -1.8), height up to 3.9, a stone mortar and a pestle (stone/logDark) at front left around (-1.7, 0.15, 1.2) with a small broom (logDark handle, carveYellow bristles), and a couple of boulders (stone) at the back right. Props keep to the circle of radius 2.9 and avoid the hut, legs and stair.
parts.attaches: All pieces stand on groundTop (y=0.15, sinking slightly). The fence opens on the fenceGapCentre line (z+). Static scenery, so ride hut for the rest pose.

calls.reasoning:
I'm sketching a spec for Baba Yaga's hut on chicken legs as a Slavic folk art diorama, and weighing whether it should be static or rigged. Since the chicken legs make it creature-like, I'm leaning toward a simple skeleton: a root for the hut and joints for the legs, perhaps the door as well. I still need to settle the joint hierarchy, starting with a base at the hips and then the leg joints, before I can set the parent relationships.

I'm settling the hut's dimensions and the diorama base next, along with a fence of skulls and a few mushrooms. I've split the model into parts, starting with the chicken legs that reach up to the floor mount and then the log cabin body with its carved door and window.

I'm breaking the hut into six parts: legs, cabin, facade with the door and window, roof, ground, and a fence with props. I'm weighing how to split the cabin's walls from the front ornamentation, and I'm budgeting the polygon count across the pieces.

I'm settling the hut's sizes now: the cabin is about 2.4 wide and 2.6 deep, with the chicken legs set in a wide stance under it and their toes spread forward. I'm weighing whether two legs are enough to balance it or whether a pair at the back is needed too.

I'm settling the ground under the hut: a disc about three units in radius with the legs' toes resting on its top surface. I'm setting the hut floor's underside at 1.75 and sizing the base plate to about six by four and a half by six, with a fence curving around the back and sides and a gap left at the front.

I'm settling the roof as a steep gable with its ridge running front to back, sized to overhang the walls, with a carved horse-head finial at each end of the ridge. I'm also setting the stair run up to the front door.

I'm placing the stairs up to the front door, running from the threshold down to the ground in front of the hut. The legs' toes will angle outward so the gap between them stays clear for the steps, and I'm also setting the palette limit at twenty-four colors.

Still choosing the palette: folk-art reds, ochres, teal, white and black, and I'm listing the grass, log, roof and carving shades, with the leg colors added last.

Still listing the palette, now down to the last few entries: a dark ink tone for outlines, and the remaining log, roof and carving shades that bring the set toward twenty-four.

I'm working through the palette now, listing the last colors: a red shingle tone, carving shades in red, blue, yellow, white and green, then the leg yellow and orange, claw black, cream feathers, the glowing window tone, bone, mushroom red, birch white and smoke grey. I'm also starting to set the joints, with the hut root at the floor height and the hip position for the left leg.

I'm placing the chicken legs' joints: the hip at the hut's floor height, the knee angled forward, and the foot planted on the ground with the toes pointing forward.

I'm setting the toe joints for each foot, with one at the front of the foot, one mid-toe, one at the outer toe, and a back toe, each pointing in its own direction. Then I'm mirroring the same layout for the right leg, adding the door hinge and the two shutter hinges on the hut, and chaining the hip, knee, ankle and foot joints under the hut root.

I'm setting the joint parents next, with the knee under the hip, the ankle under the knee and the foot under the ankle, then placing the door hinge on the hut's front-left edge. The legs' feet rest on the ground's top surface, while the ground itself is the only part that counts as the floor. I'm also starting to set the mount points for the ground top and the hut floor.

I'm placing the front gable window and the side windows with their shutters, and I'm deciding how the front face of the roof sits relative to the door and stairs.

I'm working out the cabin wall layout, with stacked horizontal logs and corner ends that stick out a little. The front wall gets split around the door opening, so the logs run full width above the lintel and beside the door, leaving the door gap for the facade to fill.

I'm settling the wall surfaces now: the cabin builds the full front wall with the door slab and window panels laid on its face rather than cut into the logs, with the outer log surface at about 1.15 in x and 1.25 in z.

I'm placing the doorway and wall mounts, with the front wall at z 1.25 and the door base at the threshold. The cabin box runs from floor height 1.6 up to 3.2, with the hips tucked inside the floor beams, and the legs' tops at 1.75.

I'm now placing the roof's rear chimney with its smoke puffs, sizing the roof box to about six by four point nine by six. The ground disc spans three units out from the center. Then I'm laying out the fence and props: a ring of bone posts with skulls at a radius of 2.4, leaving a gap in front, plus a few mushrooms to the side and a birch tree at the back left.

I'm placing the ground part next: a disc with grass tufts, stepping stones leading from the stairs toward the fence gap, soil patches, and some folk flowers and roots. Then I'm adding the facade extras: the stair with its bannister, the carved door with its frame and handle, side windows with carved platbands and shutters, a glowing skull lantern above the door, and painted sun motifs on the front wall.

I'm wrapping up the budget for each part of the hut, then writing up the layout. The door belongs to the facade, the cabin and roof hang off the hut root, and the ground and props get attached to the hut so they move with it.

I'm writing the chickenLegs function now, aiming for something rich but efficient and safe. The joints for the left leg are already defined, with the hip, knee, ankle, and foot each at their set positions. I'm planning to connect those joints with capsules or rods, with the toes placed at the foot position.

Still working out the spike layout around the thigh...

Still writing the chickenLegs parts, and I'm checking the count: the spikes, tips and shin pieces are pushing past the budget, so I'm cutting the spike rows down to two per leg.

Still adding the surface details now, with rings of orange plates along the shin and the metatarsus, and a yellow foot pad at the base.

Still working out the toe geometry: the three forward toes run about half a unit long, angled inward, and I'm checking where their ends land relative to the foot. The foot pad sits slightly raised, so the toes need to clear the floor line without sinking too far.

Still tallying the part count per leg: the toes, shin pieces and the feather spikes are adding up to about 114 for both legs, which fits the budget, so I'm considering a hip ball as well.

Still writing the chickenLegs code...

Still writing the spike placement code...

I'm writing a buildFenceAndProps function that takes the context, aiming to stay within the 140-part budget. Eighteen posts with shafts, knobs, and skull parts would add up fast, so I'm considering merging geometries by colour to reduce the mesh count, adding them to the bone's hut object.

Still writing the fence helper...

Still working through the post layout: alternating heights, a shaft with its base sunk in the ground, two knobs, and a skull on top that faces inward toward the centre.

Still laying out the rails: two horizontal rails between neighbouring posts, oriented along the direction between them. Then I'll add a few wood stakes at the midpoints and place three mushrooms near the front right.

Still placing the mushrooms, each with a stem, a hemispherical cap, and small white dots. Then I'm adding a birch tree beyond the fence, with a tapered trunk, bark marks, angled branches, and leaf clumps reaching up toward 3.9.

Still writing the code for the mortar, pestle, broom, and boulders, placing each with a position and a transform matrix.

Still writing the skull details: a cranium, a jaw with ink slits for teeth, ink eye sockets with glowing pupils, and a small nose.

Still listing the palette colours for the parts: bone, ink, glow, logDark, mushroom red, white carving, birch, green carving, grass dark, stone, yellow carving, and soil.

I'm going to write buildFacade against the module's Ctx type, using it as given rather than declaring it. I'll lay out a few small helpers for boxes and cylinders built from b.part and THREE geometries, aiming for roughly 150 parts. The front wall sits at z=1.25, and I'm starting to place the door on it.

I'm working out the door's geometry: the hinge sits at x=0.42, so the door spans from there back toward -0.42, and I'm splitting it into four planks that ride the door joint. Next I'm setting up the lintel, posts, and a small hood above the door, all tight against the 3.1 height limit.

I'm placing a skull lantern on a bracket in front of the pediment, just above the landing and below the hood. Then I'm adding a cream rushnyk panel with red zigzags beside the door at x=0.85, clear of the platband and the side windows.

Now I'm setting up the side windows at x=±1.17, each with a pane, a platband frame, and a row of red scallops along the top. The shutters swing open flat against the wall on either side, with yellow flowers on the green panels.

Next I'm laying out the staircase: a landing slab at the top of the porch, then five treads stepping down toward the ground, each one a bit lower than the last.

I'm settling on the stair build: each tread becomes a solid block running down to the ground, with the top face sitting at its step height. The risers will get small yellow dots as decoration, and I still need to add a support post under the landing so it doesn't float.

Still working out the bannister posts and rail along the staircase...

Still sorting out the rail and post layout along the stairs. The posts will be vertical rods rising from each tread, with a red knob on top of each, and the end posts get a larger carved horse-head.

Still adding the door's ink outline, a backing plate and strap hinges across the planks, placed on the door joint.

Still writing the sun rosette: I'm building it from stacked flat disks, an ink base, then yellow and red layers, with small rays set around the rim.

Still working out the rays around the sun rosette, with each one angled outward from the center. Now I'm placing the white scallops along the blue door posts and the yellow dots between them.

Still working out the hood above the door, a thin triangular piece spanning the lintel.

Still working out the lantern: I'm weighing where its bracket can attach without clashing with the hood above the door.

Still working out the skull lantern: a bone-colored sphere head with a jaw, nose, and teeth, and glowing eyes set on the front face.

Still placing the rushnyk panel beside the door: a cream board with three small red zigzag triangles stacked down it, red end stripes, and cream fringe at the bottom.

I'm placing the rushnyk panel's triangles and border so they sit flush against the front wall, then moving on to the side windows at x = ±1.15, with an ink frame plate just outside the wall surface.

Still working out the side windows: the pane, the blue platband around it, and the white muntins.

Still placing the side windows: the ink plate, the blue platband bars, the glowing pane, and the white muntins, with red scallops along the top.

Still working out the shutters and flowers: each one is a thin green panel beside the side window, with a yellow disc and a small red centre as the flower.

Still writing the helper functions for the flowers and shutters...

Still writing the box helpers and the stair tread loop...

Still adding the riser decorations, top slabs and dark blocks under each tread...

Still working out the landing's support: a dark plank riser filling the gap under the landing, so the stair doesn't look hollow from the side.

Still working out the landing's front board and the rails along the staircase, with a rod on each side and a red knob on top of every post.

Still tallying the part counts for the door, frame, windows and stairs, and they're running near the 150 target.

I'm trimming the part count now, dropping the side-bar dots and riser discs and keeping one flower with a centre per shutter, which brings the estimate toward 160.

I'm working out the roof for the hut: the ridge sits at the center and the eaves overhang the walls, so the slope has to keep dropping past the wall edge.

I'm checking the roof geometry: the slope runs from the ridge down to the eave edge at x=±1.65, which puts the roof bottom at y=3.15 and leaves a small open gap under the eaves at the sides. I'll close that gap with a soffit board and a thicker underside slab.

I'm working out the slope's direction for each side of the roof: the down-slope vector, the outward normal, and a rotation about z that keeps the local x-axis running along the pitch. The slope length comes out to about 2.1, which I'll use for laying out the shingle rows from near the ridge down to the eave.

Writing shingle rows...

Still working through the scallop layout: I'm merging the flat cylinder edges for each row into one geometry per color, keeping the count within budget.

Still working out how the slope rotation carries over to each piece: rotating about z by -s·a keeps every slope-aligned part lined up with the roof, so boxes, normals, and the scallop cylinders all follow the same orientation. I'll bake each part's transform into its geometry, then group the results by color so they can be merged into a few draw calls.

I'm sketching the gable front as a solid triangular board sitting at the roof underside, and I'm weighing its base width and where the apex lands against the ridge height.

I'm settling the gable triangle's corners against the roof underside: a base half-width of 1.45 at y=3.2 and an apex at 4.33, which tucks just under the ridge. The board gets extruded along z with zero thickness.

Now I'm laying out the gable board's vertical seams, spaced evenly across the triangle and clipped to its slanted edges. I'll give the back gable a plainer treatment with lighter boards, then start on the round window.

I'm placing the round window at about y=3.65 so its outer rays stay inside the gable's triangle, since at that height the triangle is still wide enough to hold them.

I'm laying out the barge boards along both rafters at z=1.77, sized to the slope length with a thin depth and kept at the roof's outer edge. I'll hang small triangular teeth from their lower side as a zigzag trim.

I'm now picking the colors for the teeth: alternating red, blue, and white along each side, about ten per side and merged into three parts. They'll be flattened cones hanging down below the barge board, since the fringe drops in the gable plane rather than along the roof normal.

I'm sorting out the teeth's placement: each cone points straight down, squashed thin in z, sitting just under the barge board and spaced along the slope. The board itself is a thin slope-aligned strip, and the fringe will read as an overhang in front of the gable even though a small gap remains.

I'm adding rosettes at the eaves and a pendant hanging from the apex, with the pendant's stick and diamond kept short so they clear the window. After that I'll give the back barge a plain logDark strip and finish with the konyok finial at the front ridge.

Still working on the konyok head: it's a profile in the zy plane, with a neck rising and the head tilting forward, sized to about half a unit in each direction.

Still writing the horse head profile for the konyok: I'm tracing its outline point by point, from the back of the neck around the throat, muzzle, forehead, and ear, making sure the polygon doesn't cross itself.

Still working out the horse head outline: I'm placing the throat, muzzle, and ear points so the polygon's edges run in order without crossing. Next I'll set the thickness and position the head so its base rests on the ridge beam.

I'm placing the konyok head at about y=4.58, which keeps its base buried in the ridge beam while the ear stays just under the limit.

I'm placing the konyok head further forward, scaling its outline so the tip stops right at the front edge of the roof, and I'm working out the back finial's orientation by taking the cross product of its axes.

Still working on the konyok's mane: I'm shaping a thin red panel along the neck's crest edge with a notched outline, so it reads as the carved mane.

Still writing the mane outline: a zigzag red band along the neck's crest, with its teeth rising above the head line.

I'm placing the konyok's eyes and cheek rosette: small ink discs on each side at the forward part of the head, with a yellow disc on the cheek.

I'm adding the chimney on the back side of the roof, a stone-colored box that sits partly buried in the slope, and I'm checking that its top stays under the height limit.

I'm picking the mortar color for the chimney, a darker stone tone, and adding horizontal bands at intervals so it reads as masonry. The cap will be a thin dark box near the top, and I'm checking whether the smoke puffs stay under the height limit.

I'm checking the chimney's smoke puffs against the height limit, and the cap I had in mind would put them above 4.9, so I'm considering lowering the chimney cap so the puffs stay within the limit.

I'm laying out the chimney's top: the body runs up to about 4.58, with a thin dark cap just above it, and the smoke puffs start right over that cap so they stay near the height limit. Next I'm placing a small dark flue opening at the very top, then moving on to the core roof slabs, which will be slope-aligned boxes that give the roof its underlying thickness.

I'm laying out the core slab's position and thickness, then spacing six shingle rows along the slope, each about 0.4 long and overlapping its neighbor a little, with the rows' lower edges set just below each one's center.

Still laying out the scallops: they sit at each row's lower edge, spread across the roof's width, and I'm checking how far each one overlaps the next.

I'm settling the scallop row sizes so the last one's reach stays within the eave limit at x=1.65: rows spaced at 0.31 with 0.4 length, the final row's lower edge at 1.95. Next I'm turning to the moss patches.

I'm adding moss patches on the upper faces of the shingle rows, sized small and set at varied spots across the roof. Then I'm turning to the soffit and the eave underside, where I still need to work out the surface height at the wall.

I'm checking the eave edge: the core slab's underside sits a bit above the wall plate, so there's a small gap, and I want a fascia board at each eave end to close it.

I'm sizing the core slab and shingle rows so they fit under the eave limit, and I'm accepting a slight tolerance at the underside. I'll add a logDark purlin beam along z under the core, positioned at x=±1.3 where the surface sits about y=3.43.

I'm placing the barge teeth along the rafter edge, starting at the eave and stepping up the slope in even intervals.

I'm working out how the barge teeth are colored and spaced: the fringe cones point straight down under the board, with red, white, and blue cycling along each side, and the board itself will be blue.

I'm settling the gable's back side with a plain dark strip, and I'm skipping the teeth there. Next I'm building the slope transform so each part sits on the roof plane, then merging the pieces into a few colored geometries.

Still writing the helper that places each piece in world space and groups the geometry by color, merging it into a few draw calls.

Still writing the rosette rays: I'm placing them around the window center at a fixed radius and angling each one outward so it points away from the middle.

I'm laying out the window rays: a yellow ring, ink discs, and a glowing pane with a cross of muntins over it. The rays start at a radius of about 0.37 from the window center and point outward, but the top one would run into the gable edge near y=4.1.

I'm laying out the gable's plank seams: vertical strips spaced along the front face, each one trimmed to the slanted top edge, with the window's overlap still to sort out.

I'm placing the window's layers just in front of the gable face, with the ink disc, yellow ring, pane, and muntins stacked in small z steps so they don't z-fight. For the back gable I'll use a plain roof-wood triangle with a few dark seams, and a dark strip for the back fringe.

Still writing the bucket helper: each piece gets a world transform from position and rotation, then goes into a per-color list so it can be merged later.

Still writing the konyok's extrusion code, scaling its outline points and placing the result on the ridge.

Still writing the konyok head: I'm extruding its outline and placing the mane, eyes, and cheek rosette with cylinders oriented along x.

Still writing the konyok details: a pair of yellow dots on the mane, then a small logDark pendant hanging from the apex, with its stick and octahedron kept clear of the window rays.

Still writing the rosette: I'm layering ink, red, and white discs at small z steps, plus a few short petals to round out the look.

Still writing the rosette and ridge setup: I'm adding a few white dots around the disc, then placing eave rosettes at the front corners and a long logDark ridge beam over the roof's peak.

Still writing the ridge beam setup: I'm adding a row of small cubes along its top and a soffit with fascia ends at the eaves, then merging the pieces into the colored buckets.

Still writing the moss helper: each patch gets placed on a shingle row's upper face at a set slope position, with a small box sized to the row width.

Still writing the moss patches: each one sits on a row's upper face at a set slope position, with the row lengths and heights worked out so the rows overlap cleanly.
